title: What is React Query
description: Understand React Query and its role in managing server state.

data.text: **React Query** (now called TanStack Query) is a data-fetching and state management library built specifically for **server state** â€” data that lives on a server and changes independently of your React application. It handles caching, background refetching, deduplication, and stale-data management so you can focus on building features.
Understanding the difference between server state and client state is fundamental to using React Query correctly.

data.title: React Query Is Not a Global Store
data.text: React Query is not a replacement for Redux, Zustand, or Context API. It solves a completely different problem: managing asynchronous server data. You still use useState for UI state like modals, form inputs, and sidebar toggles.

Before React Query, developers managed server data with a combination of useState, useEffect, and manual caching. This approach had well-known problems: stale data, loading loops, race conditions, and memory leaks. React Query solves all of these with a small set of hooks and sensible defaults.

data.title: Problems React Query Solves
items: **Stale data**: Data that hasn't been updated in a while is automatically refetched
**Duplicate requests**: Multiple components requesting the same data share a single network call
**Caching complexity**: No need to manually manage a cache invalidation schedule
**Loading and error states**: useQuery returns isLoading, isError, and error out of the box
**Background updates**: Data is refreshed silently in the background so the UI stays current

data.title: What React Query Does For You
items: **Caching** â€” Stores query results in memory. Subsequent renders with the same queryKey return cached data instantly.
**Background Refetching** â€” Automatically re-fetches data in the background when the window regains focus, the component re-mounts, or the network reconnects.
**Stale Time** â€” Configurable window during which data is considered fresh and not refetched.
**Garbage Collection** â€” Unused cache entries are automatically removed after a configurable time (gcTime, formerly cacheTime).
**Deduplication** â€” If two components request the same data simultaneously, only one network request is made.

terms.definition: Data stored on a remote server that your application fetches, creates, updates, or deletes. It persists independently of the user's current session or browser tab.
Data stored locally within your application â€” such as form inputs, UI toggles, modal visibility, and selected items. Managed by useState, useReducer, or similar tools.
A unique identifier (usually an array) for a query. React Query uses query keys to look up cached data and determine whether to refetch. Example: ['users', userId]
The duration (in milliseconds) that data is considered fresh. While data is fresh, React Query will not refetch it. Default is 0 â€” meaning data is stale immediately.

data.text: React Query manages server state. It does not replace your component state management library for UI concerns.
data.attribution: Tanner Linsley, Creator of TanStack Query

data.text: React Query is often misunderstood. Here is a clear list of what it is NOT designed to replace:

items: **Redux / Zustand / Jotai**: For global client state, keep using your preferred library
**React Router**: For navigation and routing, use a router â€” React Query only fetches data
**Form libraries**: Use React Hook Form or Formik for forms; React Query only fetches the initial data
**Local state**: Keep using useState for modals, sidebars, selected items, and form inputs

data.title: Classify Your App's State
data.description: Take an existing React application you have built (or a simple Todo app) and list every piece of state it manages. For each piece, classify it as 'server state' or 'client state'. Identify which pieces React Query could manage and which should stay with useState.
steps: List all state variables in your application (e.g., todos, filter, modalOpen, isLoading)
Mark each as 'server state' or 'client state'
For each server state piece, write the queryKey you would use in React Query
For each client state piece, explain why React Query is not appropriate
Identify any piece that was previously fetched with useEffect + useState
data.expectedOutcome: A clear categorization of all state in your app with justification for each classification. You should be able to confidently say which pieces belong in React Query and which belong in component state.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: React Query (TanStack Query) manages server state â€” data fetched from a backend
It is not a replacement for Redux or useState â€” those manage different concerns
It automatically handles caching, refetching, deduplication, and garbage collection
Server state changes independently of your React app â€” React Query keeps it in sync
Client state (modals, form inputs) stays with useState or your preferred library
data.takeaway: React Query fills the gap between your React app and your backend â€” handling all the hard problems of server state automatically.

data.title: What is React Query? â€” FAQ

items.question: Is React Query still called React Query?
items.answer: The library was renamed to TanStack Query to reflect its expansion beyond React. The package name on npm is still @tanstack/react-query, and the hooks are still useQuery, useMutation, etc. Many people still call it 'React Query' informally.

items.question: Do I need a backend to use React Query?
items.answer: No. React Query works with any async function â€” even one that returns a Promise resolving to local data. It is most useful with REST or GraphQL APIs, but works with WebSockets, IndexedDB, or any async source.

items.question: Can I use React Query with Next.js?
items.answer: Yes. In Next.js App Router, useQuery runs on the server during SSR/RSC by default in recent versions, or you can use it client-side with 'use client'. The cache persists across requests when using the server-side features.

items.question: Is React Query better than SWR?
items.answer: Both are excellent. React Query (TanStack Query) has a larger API surface with more options (mutations, infinite queries, optimistic updates), while SWR is lighter weight. Choose React Query if you need the full feature set.
